interpretation.diagram_classification: cosmological / meteorological diagram: wind rose (twelve winds) arranged around a central human head, in the tradition of the medieval 'wind wheel' or 'head of the world' (microcosm-macrocosm) diagrams
interpretation.interpretation: The diagram is a twelve-part wind rose. A circle divided into twelve radial sectors lists the winds in red, each with a second name in black (in most cases the Greek name of the same wind). Red names read: SUBSOLANOS (east), EURUS, EURO AUSTER, AUSTER, AUSTRO AFRICUS, AFRICUS, FABONIUS, CHORUS, CIRCIUS, SERTENTRIO/SEPTENTRIO and AQUILO, UULTURNUS. Black names read: apoliotes (for the east wind), eurus, euronotus (read in Step 1 as "euro non"), notus, libonotus (read as "liborus"), lips, zephyrus, argestes (read as "arger ir"), thrascias (read as "marci ur"), aparctias (read as "apar cias"), boreas (read as "bore as"), caecias (read as "cecias"). This is the dodecapartite system of winds known from Isidore of Seville (De natura rerum, Etymologiae XIII) and Bede, with Latin and Greek names paired. The head in the central ring is a human head in profile with a cap-like covering, placed where the diagram's axis meets. It probably stands for the world or the human being at the centre of the winds, in the microcosm/macrocosm tradition, or it may be a simple ornamental central face. The twelve knot-ornament triangles at the ends of the radial lines mark the twelve wind directions on the rim. The framing orange ring closes the circle of the horizon or of the world. The Insular-style interlace suggests a manuscript from the Insular or Carolingian milieu.
interpretation.evidence: Textual: the transcribed names SUBSOLANOS, EURUS, AUSTER, AFRICUS, FABONIUS, CHORUS, CIRCIUS, AQUILO, UULTURNUS, together with the black Greek-derived names (apolio tes, eurus, lips, zephi rus, bore as), are standard wind names. Visible: twelve radial lines and twelve knot triangles give a twelve-fold division, and the central ring holds a head in profile. External: wind diagrams in the Isidorian and Bedan tradition use the twelve-wind scheme with Latin and Greek pairs, and some pair the winds with a human figure or head as a microcosm. Problems with Step 1: several black readings are uncertain and probably garbled ("euro non", "liborus", "arger ir", "marci ur", "apar cias", "cecias"). Step 1 also gave the red labels some questionable divisions, e.g. "AUSTER" for the sector near the right-hand horizontal, "CIRCIUS" as low certainty, and "SERTENTRIO" and "AQUILO" as separate sectors where the red text partly runs across sector boundaries. Step 1 also treated the red and black texts as 'inside' the sectors by naming the sectors after the red text. The identification of the head and the exact assignment of names to compass directions are not certain.

interpretation.interpretation: The circular layout with a central point and radial divisions expresses the twelve directions of the horizon around an observer or around the world. The knot triangles on the rim function as directional markers, with the four yellow ones (top, bottom, left, right) probably marking the four cardinal directions and the eight blue-grey ones marking the intermediate winds. The colour distinction supports a hierarchy of four principal winds and eight secondary winds, as in the Isidorian scheme.
interpretation.evidence: Visible: four yellow knot triangles at top, bottom, left and right, and eight blue-grey knot triangles at intermediate positions, are recorded in Step 1 entries 3 to 14. External: the four-plus-eight arrangement matches the way the twelve-wind system is built around four principal winds. The exact direction assigned to each wind is not stated in the diagram, so the cardinal reading is an inference; the orientation (which side is east) is not marked.
